query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Using an advanced powder metallurgy route—in particular, spark plasma sintering (SPS)—to process a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will refine its microstructure and suppress deleterious phase segregation, thereby enhancing its elevated‐temperature mechanical properties compared to the same alloy produced via conventional casting.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy produced by conventional casting, which typically features coarser grains, elemental segregation, and inhomogeneous phase distribution.
generation.intervention: Adopt a powder metallurgy processing route utilizing SPS to rapidly sinter pre-alloyed powders under controlled atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Processing under an inert atmosphere with optimized sintering temperature and time to maintain phase stability; mechanical performance to be evaluated in the operating temperature range of approximately 800–1200 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain structure and a more uniform distribution of alloying elements, leading to suppression of coarse precipitates and reduced segregation.
generation.mechanism: The rapid heating and short dwell time in SPS limit grain growth and minimize phase segregation, resulting in a fine-grained, more homogeneous microstructure. This refined microstructure is expected to hinder grain-boundary sliding and improve creep resistance and yield strength at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The SPS-processed alloy will display significantly improved elevated-temperature mechanical properties, such as increased yield strength and enhanced creep resistance, relative to the cast alloy. Although a precise quantification is uncertain, an improvement on the order of approximately 10–20% in key metrics is anticipated.
generation.baseline: Properties of the alloy produced via conventional casting, with its characteristic coarse microstructure and elemental inhomogeneity leading to lower high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention is expected to be confined to processing conditions that maintain compositional homogeneity and phase stability, and for alloys meeting the high-entropy criteria (with titanium and nickel as primary constituents). Deviations in processing parameters (e.g., sintering temperature, dwell time) or alloy composition outside the defined high-entropy range may not yield the predicted benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the mechanical property improvements and the microstructural changes are uncertain due to potential scalability issues and sensitivity to exact processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy: one group produced via conventional casting and a second group processed using powder metallurgy with SPS. Characterize microstructures (grain size and elemental distribution) using scanning electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction. Conduct elevated-temperature mechanical tests (yield strength and creep resistance) over the 800–1200 °C range.
measurements: Yield strength testing at elevated temperatures
Creep resistance evaluation under controlled temperature conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-processed samples do not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., less than a 10% increase in yield strength and creep resistance) and do not exhibit a notably refined microstructure compared to the cast samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
